messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 59
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Police Officer
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 45

She is 59, a Middle Eastern woman who has spent most of her adult life in uniform. For more than three decades, she has worked as a police officer, and she still speaks about the job with a kind of disciplined pride. She is married, the mother of grown children, and used to think of herself as someone who could absorb almost anything and keep moving. She says that before the assault, she was the one other officers came to when a scene was chaotic. She was steady, practical, hard to rattle.

The assault happens late in her shift during what is first called in as a routine disturbance. She and her partner arrive at an apartment building where shouting can be heard from the hallway. She remembers the smell of cigarette smoke, the flicker of a bad fluorescent light, the weight of her vest pressing into her shoulders as she climbs the stairs. Inside the apartment, events turn suddenly. A man she is trying to calm lunges at her with a force that surprises her. She is hit, thrown off balance, and pinned for a moment that feels much longer than it is. She remembers his face too close to hers, the heat of his breath, the shock of realizing she cannot immediately control the situation. Other officers pull him off, but by then something in her has already shifted. Later, she focuses on paperwork, photographs, protocol. She tells herself she is lucky. She goes home bruised and furious, but mostly ashamed that she had felt afraid.

In the weeks afterward, she returns to work quickly. She insists on doing so. At first she frames it as professionalism, but she begins to notice that her body reacts before her mind can catch up. Calls involving domestic disputes make her palms sweat inside her gloves. In apartment hallways she scans every doorway, every pair of hands, every sudden movement. If a man raises his voice, she feels a jolt through her chest, as if she is back in that room. She starts sleeping lightly, waking at the smallest sound. When her husband rolls over in bed unexpectedly, she startles so hard that he apologizes, confused. She tells him she is fine, just tired.

Sleep becomes something she dreads. When she does drift off, she dreams of being trapped under weight, unable to breathe or reach her radio. She wakes with her heart pounding and has to sit on the edge of the bed to remind herself where she is. Some mornings she goes straight to the shower and stands under very hot water, trying to wash away the feeling that the assault is still on her skin. She begins leaving the television on at night because silence makes her too aware of every creak in the house.

At work, she notices changes she does not like in herself. She becomes sharper with younger officers, especially if they are slow to respond. She positions herself near exits in briefing rooms and restaurants. She avoids volunteering for certain calls, then feels humiliated by her own avoidance. The apartment building where the assault occurred remains in her district, and even driving past it tightens her throat. If dispatch sends her nearby, she feels angry before she even arrives. She tells herself to get over it. She has worked assaults, shootings, child deaths. She cannot understand why this one moment keeps returning uninvited.

Her husband sees more than she intends. He notices that she checks the locks multiple times before bed and that she no longer enjoys family gatherings. She used to host holidays, cooking for everyone, filling the house with relatives, Arabic music, and loud conversation. Now she finds the noise overwhelming. If people stand too close behind her in the kitchen, she loses her train of thought. She begins retreating to the bedroom during visits, claiming she has a headache. Her family interprets this at first as stress or aging, and she lets them. Part of her worries that if she explains, they will hear weakness in the story instead of injury.

What troubles her most is the change in how she sees herself. She has built her identity around competence and control, and now she mistrusts both her environment and her own reactions. On edge nearly all the time, she feels older than 59. She cries in private, often in her car before going into the house, then wipes her face and composes herself. She avoids mirrors when changing clothes because the fading marks from the assault had once made the event feel too real, and now even without them she still carries the scene inside her. She says she knows, logically, that she survived and that the man is gone. But her body does not seem to believe it. Even now, months later, she moves through the world as though danger is only one sudden movement away.
